web_title: 3. Unit Economics, Distribution Mechanics & the ₹100 Waterfall
question: How does Kody Technolab distribute its robots and software, and what happens to every ₹100 of revenue before it reaches Free Cash Flow?

epigraph.quote: Revenue is vanity, operating margin is sanity, and free cash flow after working capital is reality.
epigraph.author: Forensic Accounting Maxim

web_blocks.html: Kody's balance sheet nearly tripled while its sales surged. To see why, we must trace its distribution channels and cash conversion. Kody sells through three paths. First, it runs direct B2B and B2G sales in India for software, Athena, and Dasher [5]. Second, it uses a UAE joint venture, Falcon Tech Robotics LLC (with Platinum Group), and Kody Middle East Holding LLC to reach Gulf malls and clinics [6]. Third, Kody Media Limited places Odigo robots under Robot-as-a-Service (RaaS) and pDOOH ad contracts [2, 6].

web_blocks.title: Why RaaS & Backward Integration Change Unit Economics

web_blocks.html: In software or upfront hardware sales, the buyer pays on Day 1. Under RaaS and pDOOH, Kody removes the client's upfront cost [4]. Instead, Kody finances the robot parts, books the unit on its own fixed-asset ledger, and waits for monthly fees or ad sales to pay it back [4, 7]. Kody also invested in World EMS Private Limited to handle bulk PCB and robot assembly [7]. As a result, Fixed Assets plus CWIP jumped from ₹15 Cr (Mar 2025) to ₹68 Cr (Mar 2026) and ₹86 Cr (Sep 2026) [1]. By H1 FY27, depreciation quadrupled YoY from ₹1 Cr to ₹4 Cr, while OPM fell to 19% [1].

notes.cogs: Statutory filings aggregate COGS, payroll, and SG&A under total operating expenses (₹56.0 Cr).
notes.employee_cost: Included within consolidated operating expenses (₹56.0 Cr).

web_blocks.html: The deterministic ₹100 waterfall above reconciles every rupee of FY26 consolidated revenue (₹80.0 Cr) through to Free Cash Flow [1]. Operating expenses absorbed ₹70.00 per ₹100 of sales, leaving ₹30.00 in Operating EBITDA (₹24.0 Cr) and ₹21.25 in Net Profit (₹17.0 Cr) [1]. Yet working-capital absorption and non-cash items reduced Cash Flow from Operations to just ₹15.00 per ₹100 of revenue (₹12.0 Cr), while ₹81.25 per ₹100 of Capex (₹65.0 Cr) pushed Free Cash Flow to -₹66.25 per ₹100 (-₹53.0 Cr) [1].

web_blocks.title: Working Capital Friction: The 192-Day Receivable Bottleneck

web_blocks.html: Working capital absorption is Kody's sharpest unit-level red flag. In FY25, Debtor Days sat at an already high 177 days [1]. Working Capital Days stood at 62 days [1]. By March 2026, Debtor Days stretched to 192 days [1]. More than six months of sales sat uncollected on the balance sheet. Working Capital Days tripled to 197 days [1]. As a result, FY26 Operating Cash Flow was just ₹12 Cr against ₹24 Cr of EBITDA and ₹17 Cr of PAT [1]. Unless collections speed up, growth will keep requiring outside debt or equity.

Note also the role of Other Income in FY26. Non-operating income added ₹7 Cr, or ₹8.75 per ₹100 of sales [1]. That cash yield came largely from unspent preferential funds sitting in deposits. Core operations alone generated ₹19 Cr of PBT before Other Income [1]. By H1 FY27, Other Income added ₹3 Cr more on ₹10 Cr of PBT, showing continued reliance on treasury returns [1].

web_blocks.title: Unit-Economics Litmus Test for RaaS & pDOOH
paragraphs: Each Odigo or Athena unit under RaaS must earn enough monthly cash margin to pay back its build cost within 18 to 24 months. Receivables must also drop below 90 days. Until CFO/EBITDA recovers above 75% and FCF turns positive without equity raises, unit economics remain unproven at scale.

web_blocks.html: Why the Waterfall Matters for Investors: In pure software businesses, ₹21.25 of Net Profit per ₹100 of revenue usually converts into ₹20+ of Free Cash Flow because capex is minimal. At Kody Technolab, heavy RaaS fleet capitalization, World EMS inventory build-up, and 192-day customer receivables flip that conversion negative [1, 7]. Until debtor days fall below 120 and capex intensity moderates, every incremental rupee of hardware-led revenue requires external financing rather than generating surplus owner cash [1]. Tracking that cash bridge quarterly separates genuine compounding from accounting growth.

book_paragraphs: To see whether Kody Technolab's business model is a compounding flywheel or a capital trap, you and I have to follow ₹100 of consolidated FY26 revenue from the top line all the way down to Free Cash Flow. On the surface, the FY26 profit-and-loss statement looks deceptive in its neatness: out of ₹80 crore in sales, ₹56 crore went to operating expenses, leaving ₹24 crore in operating profit—a 30% EBITDA margin. Subtract ₹3 crore for depreciation and ₹2 crore for interest, add ₹7 crore of Other Income, and you arrive at ₹26 crore of pre-tax profit and ₹17 crore of net profit.

Now strip away the accounting polish and look at the cash register. Of that ₹30 per ₹100 of operating EBITDA, only ₹15 per ₹100—just ₹12 crore in total—actually arrived in Kody's bank account as Cash Flow from Operations. Where did the other half go? It vanished into uncollected customer bills. Debtor days stretched from 177 days in March 2025 to 192 days in March 2026, while total working capital days tripled from 62 days to 197 days.

Then comes the capex bill. In FY26, Kody spent roughly ₹65 crore on capital expenditure—₹81.25 for every ₹100 of revenue—and ₹86 crore in total investing cash outflows. Put ₹15 of operating cash inflow next to ₹81.25 of capex, and you get Free Cash Flow of minus ₹66.25 per ₹100 of revenue, or minus ₹53 crore in absolute terms. The only reason the company's cash balance rose by ₹39 crore was ₹113 crore of financing inflows from preferential shares and convertible warrants.

Why is the model suddenly so hungry for capital? Because Kody changed how it sells. In software consulting, the client pays for your engineers' time every month. In Robot-as-a-Service and programmatic DOOH advertising through Kody Media and Falcon Tech Robotics, Kody builds the robot—often through its World EMS manufacturing tie-up—puts the hardware onto its own balance sheet as a fixed asset, and hopes to collect monthly ad-tech or subscription fees over the next several years.

In the first half of FY27, we saw the next chapter of that math play out. Revenue surged 97% year-on-year to ₹62 crore, proving there is real commercial demand. Yet operating margins fell to 19%, depreciation quadrupled from ₹1 crore to ₹4 crore, borrowings jumped from ₹8 crore to ₹27 crore, and net profit barely budged at ₹5 crore. That is the exact tension you and I must keep front and center: Kody has proven it can manufacture and deploy robots, but it has not yet proven that those deployments generate fast enough cash payback to fund their own growth.

Let us test the unit economics of a single Odigo pDOOH robot on paper so you can see the payback clock clearly. When Kody or Kody Media builds an Odigo unit—combining dual 32-inch screens, LiDAR sensors, onboard compute, battery pack, and chassis—and places it in a mall under a Robot-as-a-Service or ad-revenue-share model, the cash outflow happens upfront. Every month, the robot must earn enough net contribution from programmatic advertising slots or client subscription fees to cover field maintenance, cellular connectivity, mall revenue-share, and depreciation, with enough left over to recover the initial hardware cost.

In an ideal steady state, if a fleet reaches high utilization and ad-fill rates, the marginal cost of serving an additional ad impression is near zero, and operating leverage kicks in powerfully. In the ramp-up phase, however, you pay 100% of the depreciation and field-support costs from Day 1 while ad sales and client collections lag behind. That timing mismatch is written all over Kody's FY26 and H1 FY27 statements: fixed assets plus CWIP climbed to ₹86 crore, depreciation quadrupled in H1 FY27, and operating cash flow lagged net profit by ₹5 crore in FY26.

There is also a second distribution friction we cannot ignore: the working capital gap between India and the UAE. Exporting hardware through Falcon Tech Robotics or billing domestic institutional clients for custom AI and surveillance deployments stretches the receivable cycle. At 192 debtor days, Kody is effectively extending more than six months of free trade credit to its customers and channel partners. Until that collection cycle tightens and capex moderates relative to operating cash flow, every ₹100 of revenue will continue to look far stronger on the P&L than it does in the bank.

Look closely at the cash conversion ratio in Screener's historical table: CFO before tax divided by operating profit stood at 63% in FY25 and 83% in FY26, yet after-tax CFO was only ₹12 crore against ₹17 crore of net profit and ₹24 crore of EBITDA. That gap between pre-tax and post-tax cash conversion—compounded by ₹65 crore of capex—is why financing inflows of ₹113 crore were indispensable in FY26.

In short, Kody's unit economics have moved from high-margin, quick-cash software to capital-heavy, slow-collecting hardware and media. Until the company proves that deployed Odigo and Medigo units generate steady post-tax cash faster than they depreciate, every rupee of top-line growth carries a heavy balance-sheet price tag.

Keep that ₹100 waterfall handy as you read the rest of this dossier. Whenever a company's operating cash flow is ₹15 per ₹100 of sales while capex is ₹81.25 per ₹100, growth is not self-funding; it is externally financed.

book_callouts.title: The RaaS Balance-Sheet Paradox
book_callouts.text: Switching customers from upfront purchases to monthly RaaS subscriptions accelerates adoption, but it turns an asset-light software firm into a balance-sheet lender. Watch whether debtor days fall below 120 and FCF turns positive before celebrating top-line growth.
